results.summary: This is an 8-bit CPU trainer with an accumulator, four working registers, and an ALU supporting add, subtract, logic, and shift operations. It is controlled by feeding opcodes and immediate data through the ui pins and toggling load and execute inputs, with results shown on a 7-segment display or as binary. The design requires a 10 kHz clock and a 7-segment display for output. Silicon testing confirmed operation from 10 kHz to 50 MHz, though a known bug in the subtract-with-borrow instruction adds the carry flag instead of subtracting it.

TinySnake is a simple game where a three-segment snake moves around a 7-segment display, with direction randomized by an LFSR. The speed is set via the ui input pins, and the snake's position is stored in three 3-bit registers. It requires only the on-board 7-segment display and a 10 kHz clock. A limitation is that changing from a slower to a faster speed may cause a delay because the speed comparison uses an equality check rather than greater-than-or-equal.

This design bundles several digital structures: a 4-bit counter, positive and negative edge trigger circuits, an LFSR for pseudo-random sequences, and multiple pulse counters with trigger circuits. It is tested by connecting external inputs and observing outputs on the uo and uio pins. The documentation is brief and does not specify external hardware requirements beyond basic input/output connections. The project appears to be an educational collection of common digital building blocks.

This is a 4-bit adder built from four full adder stages, with the sum latched by D flip-flops on each clock rising edge. The carry-out is not latched and is available directly. It is tested by applying two 4-bit numbers via the ui pins and observing the sum on the uo pins, with a 1 Hz clock. External hardware needed is just LEDs to display the result.

This sequential circuit uses D flip-flops to display the name 'Andre' on a 7-segment display. It is tested by connecting the outputs to a common-cathode 7-segment display and providing a 1 Hz clock. The design requires only the 7-segment display as external hardware. The documentation is minimal and does not describe the internal state machine or character sequence in detail.

This circuit performs 4-bit addition or subtraction based on a control pin: low for addition, high for subtraction using two's complement. The binary result is output on the uo pins and can be converted to decimal via an external BCD-to-7-segment decoder for display. It is tested by providing two 4-bit numbers and toggling the control pin. The design requires a 7-segment display and decoder for easy reading of the result.

This is a parity detector that turns on an LED when an even number of its eight switch inputs are high, and turns it off for an odd number. It is built from six XOR gates and is tested by toggling the input switches and observing the parity output. No external hardware beyond the switches and LED is required. The documentation is very brief and does not include a schematic or detailed explanation.

This design implements an 8-bit binary counter and shift register using D or RS flip-flops, selectable via control inputs. It can operate as a ripple counter or a serial shift register, with outputs shown on LEDs. Testing involves providing a clock, reset, and control signals to select the mode and flip-flop type. External hardware needed is basic LEDs and switches.

This is a BCD to 7-segment encoder that converts a 4-bit BCD input into segment drive signals for a 7-segment display. It includes additional gates to control the decimal point. The design is tested by applying BCD values to the ui pins and observing the segment outputs on the uo pins. It requires a common-cathode 7-segment display for visual output.

This design provides control logic for test pads on the north side of the TTGF0p1 die, allowing configuration bits to be set and read back. It uses a config bit index and toggle signals to select and modify configuration bits, with outputs reflecting pad inputs and the selected config bit value. The design is intended for silicon testing and does not require external hardware beyond the chip's pads. The documentation is sparse and focuses on pin functions rather than a full description.
